question: What voices speak in chapter 1 (she, he, the young women), and how does each express desire and admiration?

The book is called “Song of Songs” and has been read both as love poetry between a man and a woman and as an image of the love between God and His people: what does the text of verses 1 to 4 itself highlight?
The adjective יָפֶה (yafeh, “beautiful”) appears in verses 8, 15 and 16: how is beauty affirmed by each of them to the other, and not just from one side?
She says “I am dark, yet lovely” before the gaze of the daughters of Jerusalem: how do you deal with others' gaze on your body and your story?
What signs of spring does the beloved describe when inviting his beloved to come away, in verses 10 to 13?
The refrain asks that love not be awakened “until the time is right”: what does this care suggest about the timing of love?
The word אַהֲבָה (ahavah, “love”) appears in verses 4, 5 and 7: what different faces of love do these verses show, from celebration to weakness to waiting?
“Catch for us the little foxes that ruin the vineyards”: what small things may be wearing down a relationship that matters to you?
Where and how does she seek “the one my soul loves,” and what happens before she finds him?
The scene changes to Solomon's procession on his wedding day: what contrast is there between this royal pomp and the night search of verses 1 to 4?
The verb אָהַב (ahav, “love”) is repeated in verses 1 to 4 in the phrase “the one my soul loves”: what does this repetition convey about the intensity of the search?
The beloved seeks and does not find, but rises and keeps searching: in what relationship, with God or with someone, do you need to persist in seeking?
What parts of his beloved's body does he describe in verses 1 to 7, and with what images from nature and the landscape of Israel?
He calls her a “garden locked up” and a “spring sealed up,” and then a “well of fresh water”: what do these images suggest about intimacy and exclusiveness?
The word כַּלָּה (kallah, “bride”) appears in verses 8 to 12: what change of tone is there when he begins to call her this, and also “my sister”?
“You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw”: how can words like these heal, and to whom would you need to say them?
What happens between the moment the beloved knocks at the door and the moment she goes out into the city, in verses 2 to 7?
She hesitates to open and, when she does, he is gone: what lesson about response and opportunity do readers, literal or allegorical, usually see in this scene?
The word דּוֹד (dod, “beloved”) is repeated in the young women's question in verse 9 and in her answer through verse 16: how does she describe the one who stands out “among ten thousand”?
“I sleep, but my heart is awake”: in what area of your life are you half awake, half asleep to what matters?
How does the beloved compare his beloved to the queens, concubines and maidens in verses 8 to 10?
The phrase “I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine” returns here in the reverse order of 2:16: what does this mutual belonging say about the love described in the book?
The adjective אָיֹם (ayom, “awesome, majestic”) appears in verses 4 and 10, alongside “an army with banners”: what kind of beauty does this unexpected word suggest?
He says “my dove, my perfect one, is unique”: what does it mean, in practice, to treat someone as unique in a culture of comparisons?
In what order does the beloved describe his beloved in verses 1 to 9, and what geographical places does he mention in the comparisons?
She invites her beloved to go out to the fields and vineyards in spring: what role do nature and the land have in the expression of love throughout the book?
The word תְּשׁוּקָה (teshuqah, “desire”) of verse 10 also appears in Genesis 3:16: what dialogue might there be between the two texts about desire between man and woman?
“I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me”: what place do desire and tenderness have in the relationships you value?
Who speaks in verses 8 and 9 about the little sister, and how does she herself answer in verses 10 to 12?
Love is “as strong as death” and “mighty waters cannot quench love”: how are these images usually read, both of human love and of God's love?
The word חוֹתָם (chotam, “seal”) appears twice in verse 6: what did a seal over the heart and the arm mean, and what commitment does this image ask for?
The text says whoever tried to buy love with all his wealth would be utterly scorned: what things in your life have you tried to replace with money or gifts?
